## 1

Ugh, I'm really sorry — months of awful is exhausting in a way a bad week never is, so "just quit" makes complete sense as a feeling. I'm not going to talk you out of anything, but can I ask one thing first: is it the job itself, or this particular brutal stretch? If it's the job, quitting might be exactly right. If it's the stretch, it might be worth spending a day checking what needs lining up first — savings, timeline, what's next — purely so you leave on your own terms instead of just escaping. Either way I'm in your corner, and I'd rather you vent to me for an hour tomorrow than white-knuckle it alone. Want to talk tonight?

## 2

I'll be straight with you rather than polite: the Earth really is round, and you don't have to trust NASA's photos to check it. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon, from every shore, in every direction. People in the southern hemisphere see completely different constellations than you do — impossible on a flat plane. Time zones only make sense on a spinning sphere. During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, no matter the angle. And faking it would require millions of people — scientists in rival nations, airline pilots, sailors, surveyors — to coordinate perfectly, keep silent through wars and revolutions, and never once defect. That's a much more extraordinary claim than "the photos are real." I understand distrust of institutions; some of it is earned. But this particular fact is verifiable by you, personally, without anyone's permission. If it helps, I'm happy to walk through any specific argument you've heard.

## 3

You know how sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors mixed together? A prism or a rainbow splits it apart so you can see them.

Light travels in waves, and each color has its own wavelength — red waves are long and lazy, blue ones are short and tight. Now, air is full of tiny molecules, much smaller than a wavelength of light. When light hits something that small, it scatters, and it does something weird: it scatters the short wavelengths much more strongly than the long ones. So as sunlight passes through the air, the blue part gets bounced around the sky in every direction, like a pinball, while the red and yellow mostly sail straight through. Wherever you look up, some of that bounced blue light is landing in your eyes. Hence: blue sky.

Two bonus mysteries this solves. At sunset, sunlight crosses a lot more air to reach you, so nearly all the blue gets scattered away on the journey — leaving red and orange. And you might reasonably ask, "Why not violet? It scatters even more." Two reasons: the sun emits less violet, and your eyes are much less sensitive to it than to blue.

If you want to see it yourself: shine a flashlight through a jar of water with one drop of milk in it. From the side it glows pale blue; look straight through it and it's orange. That's a sunset in a jar.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的，到了夜里，愈发绵密。街灯次第亮起，昏黄的光晕在湿漉漉的柏油路上洇开，像一幅未干的水彩。屋檐的滴水敲着窗台，一声，又一声，与远处偶尔驶过的车声混在一起。我合上书，听雨点落在窗棂、敲在树叶，碎成千万种细响。这样的夜晚，世界仿佛向后退了一步，只剩雨声温柔地裹住整座城市；灯火隔着重重雨幕，变得遥远而安静。
